question.question:
D1 — Retry mechanism: library built-in hooks or a custom inline scheduler?
Project/branch/task: main — plan "Add background job retry framework", reviewing PLAN.md.
ELI10: The job library already knows how to retry a job later with a growing delay. The plan rebuilds that from scratch inside each of five workers because the team wants to pick the exact delay curve. Most libraries let you hand them your own delay function, so you keep the curve and drop the rebuild. The stakes: a homegrown scheduler must also remember attempt counts across restarts, stop after N tries, and report failures, or jobs retry forever or vanish silently.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Either we ship five slightly different retry engines that drift and lose attempt state on a worker restart, or we discover late that the library cannot express the curve and have to rip out the hooks.
Recommendation: A because the plan admits the library has the same shape and the only stated reason to rebuild is curve control, which a backoff callback normally gives you.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=5/10, C=n/a (investigation, approves nothing)
Pros / cons:
A) Library hooks + custom curve (recommended) (human: ~1 day / CC: ~10 min)
  ✅ Attempt counts, scheduling and dead-letter handling come from code already running in production for other users of the library
  ✅ The curve lives in one backoff function that unit-tests trivially; five workers cannot drift apart
  ❌ If the hook API cannot express the curve (unverified), we fall back to B after a short spike
B) Custom inline scheduler (as planned) (human: ~3-4 days / CC: ~30 min plus ongoing upkeep)
  ✅ Total control over delay math, logging and dispatch with no library constraints
  ✅ No dependency on the library's hook contract or its future API changes
  ❌ Re-implements persistence of attempt state, max attempts and dead-lettering, each a new failure path with no production history
  ❌ Five copies of a scheduler is five places to fix the same bug
C) Investigate hook API first (bounded) (human: ~30 min / CC: ~5 min)
  ✅ Settles the one unknown (custom backoff support) before committing either way
  ✅ Cheap; produces evidence instead of an assumption
  ❌ Approves nothing; the mechanism stays undecided and this question returns
Net: Trading full control over code we must now own against reusing a scheduler the plan itself says has the same shape.

question.question:
D2 — Retry budget: what happens when a job keeps failing?
Project/branch/task: main — plan "Add background job retry framework", reviewing PLAN.md.
ELI10: Some failures are temporary (the database hiccupped) and some are permanent (the record was deleted). Retrying a permanent failure forever just burns workers and hides the bug. The plan says how long to wait between tries but never says when to stop or what to do with a job that never succeeds. A dead-letter set is a parking lot for those jobs so a human can look at them and replay them.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Unbounded retries keep poisoned jobs cycling and starve healthy ones; log-and-drop loses the job and whatever the user was waiting on with no way to replay it.
Recommendation: A because exhausted jobs are information; parking them with an alert is the only option where a tired human at 3am can see what broke and replay it.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10, C=2/10
Pros / cons:
A) Bounded + dead-letter + alert (recommended) (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min)
  ✅ Permanent failures stop consuming workers after a known number of tries and stay replayable
  ✅ An alert on the dead-letter set turns silent job loss into a visible incident
  ❌ Needs a dead-letter destination and an alert rule, both small but real plumbing
B) Bounded, log and drop (human: ~1 hour / CC: ~5 min)
  ✅ Stops infinite retries with almost no new plumbing beyond a max-attempts number
  ✅ Error log still records which job died and why
  ❌ The job is gone; replay means finding the log line and re-enqueuing by hand, if the payload was even logged
C) Unbounded (human: 0 / CC: 0)
  ✅ No job is ever dropped, so a dependency that recovers next week still gets its work done
  ✅ Zero configuration
  ❌ Poisoned jobs cycle forever, inflate the queue and mask real bugs; the usual production incident
Net: Trading a little plumbing now against job loss or queue poisoning that only shows up during an incident.

question.question:
D3 — Jitter: randomize the retry delay or keep it exact?
Project/branch/task: main — plan "Add background job retry framework", reviewing PLAN.md.
ELI10: When a shared dependency blips, hundreds of jobs fail in the same second. If they all wait exactly 2 s, then 4 s, then 8 s, they all come back at the same instant and knock the dependency over again. Jitter adds randomness to each wait so the retries spread out. It is one line in the backoff function.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Without jitter a 30-second outage turns into a rolling series of self-inflicted spikes; with jitter the curve is slightly harder to reason about in tests (you assert a range, not a value).
Recommendation: A because full jitter is the standard remedy for retry storms and costs one random call; the test asserts a bounded range.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10
Pros / cons:
A) Full jitter (recommended) (human: ~30 min incl. test / CC: ~3 min)
  ✅ Spreads retries after a shared failure so the dependency gets room to recover
  ✅ Lives inside the one backoff function approved in D1, so every worker gets it for free
  ❌ Unit tests assert a delay range instead of an exact value; slightly less legible curve
B) No jitter (human: 0 / CC: 0)
  ✅ Exact, predictable delays that are trivial to assert and to read in logs
  ✅ Nothing to add
  ❌ Correlated failures retry in lockstep, the textbook thundering herd
Net: Trading exact-value test assertions for protection against the most common retry incident.

options.label: Full jitter (recommended)
options.description: Backoff function returns random(0, base × 2^attempt). Applied once, inside the shared backoff function from D1, so all workers inherit it. Human ~30 min incl. test / CC ~3 min. ✅ Spreads correlated retries. ✅ One place, every worker. ❌ Tests assert a range, not a value. Completeness 10/10. R2, R3, R4, R7, R8 stay pending.

options.label: No jitter
options.description: Backoff function returns exactly base × 2^attempt. Human 0 / CC 0. ✅ Exact, predictable delays. ✅ Nothing to add. ❌ Correlated failures retry in lockstep. Completeness 6/10. R2, R3, R4, R7, R8 stay pending.

## Section 1: Architecture review

Flow under the approved mechanism (D1 = A):

```
enqueue(job) ──► library picks job ──► worker.handle(payload)
                                          │
                              ┌───────────┴─────────────┐
                           success                    throws
                              │                          │
                           ack/done        library retry hook: attempt n
                                                         │
                                       backoffFn(n) ──► delay d (R6 jitter? R7 cap?)
                                                         │
                                        n < maxAttempts? (R5) ── no ──► exhaustion: dead-letter? drop? alert?
                                                         │ yes
                                              reschedule at now+d ──► (loop)

processWebhookJob: HTTP POST to receiver ──► timeout/5xx ──► throws ──► RETRY ──► POST again
                                                                        ▲
                                     receiver may already have the first POST: duplicate delivery (R3)
```

Findings (most severe first):

2. **[P1] (confidence: 8/10) PLAN.md:17-19** — Retrying `processWebhookJob()` silently changes the delivery contract. Motivating text: "The existing `processWebhookJob()` flow gets rewritten as part of this change. No regression test for the prior at-most-once delivery guarantee is planned." A retry after a POST that was sent but not acknowledged (timeout, 5xx after the receiver committed) delivers the same webhook twice. At-most-once becomes at-least-once for every receiver, which is a contract change, not a test gap. Realistic production failure: receiver returns 504 under load, every webhook in flight is re-sent, receivers without dedupe double-process. Remedy: R3 (settled by one dedicated regression question in Test review, per the regression rule).
3. **[P1] (confidence: 7/10) PLAN.md:7-9** — No retry budget or exhaustion behavior. The plan names an "exponential-backoff scheduler" and nothing about max attempts, dead-lettering or alerting. A job whose failure is permanent (bad payload, deleted record) retries until the heat death of the queue, or is dropped on the floor with no record, depending on what the library does by default (unverified). Remedy: R5.
4. **[P2] (confidence: 7/10) PLAN.md:7-9** — No jitter. Five workers retrying after a shared dependency blip compute the same delays and hit it again in lockstep: a retry storm that extends the outage. Remedy: R6.
5. **[P2] (confidence: 6/10) PLAN.md:7-9** — No delay cap. Pure exponential growth at base 1 s puts attempt 10 at ~17 min and attempt 20 at ~6 days; with a budget (R5) the cap matters less, but an explicit ceiling keeps the curve legible. Medium confidence, verify this is actually an issue once the backoff function is written. Remedy: R7.
6. **[P2] (confidence: 6/10) PLAN.md:7-9** — No rollout control. All five workers switch from no-retry to retry in one deploy with no per-job-type switch to turn it back off if a receiver melts down. Medium confidence, verify this is actually an issue given the deploy tooling (not available). Remedy: R8.

Security: no auth or data-access boundary changes; retried webhook POSTs re-send the same payload to the same receiver, so no new exposure beyond duplication (R3). Distribution: no new artifact. Single point of failure: the database both stores jobs and gets re-queried on each retry (Section 4).

Question D3:
D3 — Jitter: randomize the retry delay or keep it exact?
Project/branch/task: main — plan "Add background job retry framework", reviewing PLAN.md.
ELI10: When a shared dependency blips, hundreds of jobs fail in the same second. If they all wait exactly 2 s, then 4 s, then 8 s, they all come back at the same instant and knock the dependency over again. Jitter adds randomness to each wait so the retries spread out. It is one line in the backoff function.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Without jitter a 30-second outage turns into a rolling series of self-inflicted spikes; with jitter the curve is slightly harder to reason about in tests (you assert a range, not a value).
Recommendation: A because full jitter is the standard remedy for retry storms and costs one random call; the test asserts a bounded range.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10
Pros / cons:
A) Full jitter (recommended) (human: ~30 min incl. test / CC: ~3 min)
  ✅ Spreads retries after a shared failure so the dependency gets room to recover
  ✅ Lives inside the one backoff function approved in D1, so every worker gets it for free
  ❌ Unit tests assert a delay range instead of an exact value; slightly less legible curve
B) No jitter (human: 0 / CC: 0)
  ✅ Exact, predictable delays that are trivial to assert and to read in logs
  ✅ Nothing to add
  ❌ Correlated failures retry in lockstep, the textbook thundering herd
Net: Trading exact-value test assertions for protection against the most common retry incident.
